gaps.sentence: I put ___ sugar in your tea by mistake.
gaps.explanation: 'Too much' is used before uncountable nouns like sugar; 'too sugar' is impossible.

gaps.sentence: ___ attempts were made to contact her.
gaps.explanation: 'Several' is used with countable plurals; 'much', 'little' and 'a great deal of' need uncountables.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the workforce is part-time now.
gaps.hint: pattern: ___ of + specific group; singular verb
gaps.explanation: 'Half of the workforce is ...' is the correct pattern; 'the half of' is not used in this position.

gaps.sentence: There is so ___ crime in this area that people are afraid.
gaps.explanation: 'So much' is used with uncountable nouns like crime; 'plenty' would need 'of'.

gaps.sentence: ___ the food was eaten within minutes.
gaps.explanation: 'All the food' is correct with an uncountable noun; 'whole' needs 'the whole of' and 'both' needs two separate items.

gaps.sentence: She has two children. One lives in Leeds, and ___ lives in York.
gaps.hint: one of a pair of two
gaps.explanation: 'One ... the other ...' is the pattern for exactly two; 'another' would imply more than two.

gaps.sentence: I looked everywhere, but I couldn't find my keys ___.
gaps.explanation: After a negative verb, 'anywhere' is used; 'somewhere' belongs to affirmative sentences.

gaps.sentence: Not ___ candidates applied for the position.
gaps.explanation: 'Not many' is used with countable plurals like candidates; 'not much' is for uncountables.
